I use bongs only occasionally, but that hasn't stopped me from forming a few opinions about them. Everybody is different and everybody likes what they like, and I have no argument whatsoever with folks who enjoy things differently. These are just my personal biases and unscientific suppositions, offered in no particular order:

Ice Catchers Can Break Your Downstem

Ice melts, and when it melts it falls out of the tube, often right onto downstem. The stem acts as a lever and focuses all the force against the joint, where the stem can break. If you use an ice catcher, make sure it will let only really small pieces of ice fall though.

Ice Vrs Humidity

I seem to hold a minority opinion here, but I believe that humidity, rather than cooling, is what makes the smoke smooth. Warm water works best. Ice, in my unfounded estimation, seems well suited for condensing and removing the psychoactive vapors, which is what I don't want. If I wanted to design a bong that removed all the useful stuff while leaving only the soot behind, I'd design it with a long cold tube. Warm and wet is best.

Joint Sizes Are Not Universal

Sure, a 14mm male joint is always close enough to 14mm diameter to work, but if it's too long and skinny it still won't fit into your shallow 14mm female. The industry really needs to standardize this stuff. There is an ideal angle and depth that maximizes the strength of the joint. Use that.

Tipping

Giving a long glass tube full of stinky water to stoned person is just asking for trouble. Resistance to tipping ought to be a primary design consideration.

The Safe Place

Whenever I use glassware of any kind, part of my setup includes providing an unambiguously safe spot to stash it during pauses. For most bongs, a shallow cardboard box, just the right size to keep it from tipping over, is about ideal. If you accidentally bump it, the bong falls against the side of the box, rather than all the way down to the floor.

The Three Handed Problem

Ergonomically, bongs are a design disaster. In use, you are usually expected to keep the base against the floor, your lap, or the table, tip it into an unstable position, and then use three hands - one to hold it in position, one to operate the lighter, and one to manipulate the bowl or carb. It's no wonder beginners have a hard time. Some of the things that help are bongs with wide flat bases, bowls with those little finger levers that fit just loosely enough that they won't sick, and gently tilted necks. You should be able to have a clear view of the bowl while the mouthpiece is in position against your mouth.

Cleaning

Clean glass always tastes better than dirty glass, and some bongs are a lot easier to clean than others. The easier it is to clean the more often it is cleaned, and the more often it is cleaned the better it tastes. If you want to skip cleaning that's up to you, but for god's sake, at least use fresh water for every sesh - mold and bacteria grow in that stuff and pulling it into your lungs in just crazy. If your bong is dirty, and least let it be dry and dirty. That will minimize the biohazard.

The Ideal Bong (for me)

It has just the right size, shape, height and weight so that the base fits comfortably and securely against my lap when in use. The stem is angled just right so I can see the bowl, and when I set it down there is minimal danger of tipping. The bowl is easy to reach with my finger and lifts right up, without dragging the downstem with it or threatening to come all the way off.

It's short enough to fit gracefully into the sink so cleaning is easy. It has a device inside that drives the water into a foamy froth without letting any get into my mouth, and this device cleans easily as well.

The internal air volume is maybe 80% of the maximum of my lungs. Clearing it is easy and comfortable, but it delivers full hits.

The glass is not used as an advertising billboard with some giant ugly-ass business logo on it. The glass is either pretty or plain, and the logo is in small print on the bottom of the base. The female joints are deep so everything fits, and it works great with a standard downstem.

On the sizes you can use a AA battery when buying a new piece.
Tape a magnet on the side to store the lighter between lighting and pulling the bowl.

http://www.propublica.org/documents/item/methane-contamination-of-drinking-water-accompanying-gas-well-drilling

But that study only examined 60 wells. A more recent study looked at 1,700 wells in the same area and found no relation between being close to natural gas drilling and having methane in your water.

http://www.ogj.com/1/vol-109/issue-49/exploration-development/methane-in-pennsylvania-water-full.html

Gallay shows a study by Cornell ecology professor Robert Howarth that says fracking does not reduce greenhouse gas emissions because methane is an unusually powerful greenhouse gas. But an MIT study found that Howarth's estimates of the emissions from fracking are 7 to 30 times too large.

http://m.iopscience.iop.org/1748-9326/7/4/044030/pdf/1748-9326_7_4_044030.pdf

A study by Cornell scientist Lawrence Cathles also criticizes Howarth's assumptions. (If you want more details, Howarth responded to the critics. Then Cathles responded to the response.)

Fracking opponents also cite accidents like this one: "Frack Fluid Spill in Dimock Contaminates Stream, Killing Fish." An MIT report counted up more cases.

http://m.iopscience.iop.org/1748-9326/7/4/044030/pdf/1748-9326_7_4_044030.pdf

But put that in perspective. There are at least 35,000 active hydraulic fracturing wells in the US. In other words, MIT found about one alleged problem for every 1,000 wells. Mistakes happen; one-per- thousand is about as error-free as energy production gets.

Technology will also make fracking even safer: Scientists recently invented a fracking fluid that is so safe, you can drink it.

http://www.washingtontimes.com/blog/inside-politics/2013/feb/12/colorado-gov-hickenlooper-i-drank-fracking-fluid/

http://cogcc.state.co.us/library/GASLAND%20DOC.pdf
